raw_text: Road/Street Issues covers the roadway and its fixtures: potholes, sinkholes, snow/ice, street sweeping, drainage, paving, guide rails, retaining walls, and sign work. In the 2015-2017 archive most surface work routes to DPW - Street Maintenance, paving to DOMI - Asphalt, sign and marking work to DOMI - Traffic or DOMI - TrafficShop, and water-related drainage to the Pittsburgh Water and Sewer Authority. Note the DPW->DOMI renaming during this period: the same work appears under both 'DPW - ...' and 'DOMI - ...' names.
license_note: Public information, City of Pittsburgh 311; authored routing summary.

raw_text: Traffic and Street Sign Issues (the generic 'Sign' request type) routes, perhaps surprisingly, to Permits, Licenses and Inspections in the archive, not to a DPW/DOMI traffic unit. Traffic SIGNAL work is filed under Road/Street Issues (signal maintenance -> DOMI - Traffic; new signal -> engineering). A dark traffic signal is not a dark streetlight.
license_note: Public information, City of Pittsburgh 311; authored routing summary.

raw_text: Street Light covers roadway/sidewalk lighting. Repairs to existing lights route to outside contractors -- primarily Allegheny City Electric, with some to Sargent Electric -- not to the City directly. New-light and wattage requests route to City permits/engineering, with a small share to DPW - Park Maintenance for park lighting. A dark streetlight is NOT a traffic signal outage.
license_note: Public information, City of Pittsburgh 311; authored routing summary.

raw_text: Pedestrian/Bicycle Concerns covers sidewalks, curb ramps, city steps, and bike infrastructure. Routing is split mainly between DOMI - Permits and Permits, Licenses and Inspections, with some DPW - Street Maintenance and DOMI - Streets. A vehicle parked in a bike lane is really a Parking enforcement matter (Police), even though it endangers cyclists.
license_note: Public information, City of Pittsburgh 311; authored routing summary.

raw_text: Parking covers on-street vehicles and parking infrastructure, split across very different owners. Illegal parking routes to Police - Zones 1-6; abandoned vehicles route to Police - AVU (Abandoned Vehicle Unit). Meters, permits, and garages route to the Parking Authority. The question 'parked illegally right now, or abandoned for weeks?' changes the department.
license_note: Public information, City of Pittsburgh 311; authored routing summary.

Commercial Recycling Resources and Tonnage Reporting Requirement
As spelled out by Pittsburgh City Waste & Recycling Code: §619.02(a) and §619.04(f), Allegheny County Solid Waste Code §570-17(a), and State Act 101, Section 904: Recycling is mandatory in Pittsburgh All businesses in Pittsburgh must establish a program to recycle at least three of the following types of materials: Mixed Paper – White office paper, newspaper, magazines, hardcover/softcover books, catalogs, junk mail, phone books, paperboard, and flattened corrugated cardboard Aluminum and steel – cans and bottles Plastics – bottles, jugs, jars, and tubs Glass – amber, green, and clear bottles, jugs and jars Organic waste – leaves, garden residues, shrubbery, and tree trimming The City is not able to service businesses and they are responsible for hiring a private collector for municipal waste and recyclables View list of Commercial Recycling Haulers (PDF, 121KB) Anyone collecting and transporting recyclable materials must track source, tonnages, and disposal, and make regular reports to local government All recycling tonnages must be reported to the City’s Recycling Division on a quarterly or yearly basis (business’ preference) Private haulers can provide the tonnage report to the City on behalf of their clients The City of Pittsburgh applies for State funding with these cumulative report totals and is eligible for up to $10 for every ton recycled within city limits

Zero Waste
Pittsburgh's Journey to Zero Waste
It starts with prevention or reduction, and over-consumption is a key factor. It begins in the store. Whenever possible, drive to the store to pick up the item you need to reduce your cardboard and packaging usage. Then, next in order of effectiveness is reuse. This step is effective for durable goods that still have some life. Then recycling when the item needs to be broken down into its components to be made into something else. Next is energy recovery, allowing for the collection of methane gas from landfills to be used as natural gas for heating and energy or electricity from incineration. And finally, at the bottom of the inverted pyramid – disposal.

Pre-Event Planning
Pack-In/Pack-Out: Talk with your vendors and/or fellow event coordinators to understand who, what, where and how many materials will be generated. Establish ownership of these materials and eliminate waste whenever possible. Develop and coordinate a plan for handling and recycling the materials once collected: Find out what programs or equipment are already available on-site at your venue. Existing infrastructure may be sufficient for your needs. Arrange for the storage and/or return of loaned equipment (City-owned equipment must be returned the following business day). Once you have developed your plan, be sure to actively communicate expectations/availability of recycling and disposal options with your visitors, staff and/or volunteers.
